newsitem.title: UK: Rhodium 96 use to fall as automakers cut stocks - JM.
newsitem.headline: Rhodium 96 use to fall as automakers cut stocks - JM.

text.p: Rhodium demand was forecast to fall 40,000 ounces to 419,000 ounces in 1996 as a decline in offtake by automakers outweighted higher industrial consumption, according to Johnson Matthey's Platinum 1996 Interim Review.
Published on Tuesday, the report from the world's leading refiner of platinum group metals (PGMs), said that supplies at 463,000 ounces "will substantially exceed consumption".
"Excluding stock changes the underlying trend is still one of increasing rhodium consumption, particularly in the growing vehicle markets of Asia and Latin America," the report said.

But despite "modest" rises in worldwide vehicle production in 1996 compared with 1995, rhodium purchases by the car makers were likely to fall as they worked down inventories built last year, the report said.
There would also be an increase in the amount of metal recovered from spent autocatalysts -- 47,000 ounces against 39,000 ounces last year.

Demand from rhodium's industrial end users pricipally in glass and chemicals was expected to reach its highest since 1990 at 28,000 ounces (up 11,000 ounces on 1995) and 17,000 ounces (up 4,000 ounces) respectively.
Demand from the glass industry has risen from a low of 3,000 ounces in 1993 as accumulated inventories have been worked down.
"Stocks are now lower and during 1996 there has been a substantial rise in sales of rhodium to producers of fibre glass, cathode ray tubes and high quality flat glass for LCDs," the report said.
But supplies will also rise with higher exports forecast from both South Africa and Russia.
"Overall we expect supplies to exceed demand by 44,000 ounces," the report said.
